To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the selective-attention ERP component processing negativity (PN) reflects a cerebral matching between the sensory input to the cerebral cortex and a voluntary representation of the stimulus that is to be attended.
the selective-attention effects on the ERP are larger with smaller pitch separation.

the selective-attention ERP effect called the processing negativity reflects the cerebral matching process between a sensory input and a neuronal representation of a stimulus voluntarily maintained in working memory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurophysiological mechanisms of selective attention.
the study of the neural correlates of selective attention.
the question of how the brain selects the information to which we attend, in other words, how the brain selects what is relevant and what is not.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the selective-attention process is reflected by the PN in the ERPs.
selective-attention effects are not restricted to the stimuli that are attended but also occur in a more generalized manner to the stimuli that resemble the attended stimuli.
the PN reflects a cerebral process of selective attention, but that this process is not necessarily restricted to the stimulus that is physically identical to the target.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

selective attention can be considered to be based on a cerebral representation of the stimulus or event to be attended, a representation which is continuously updated and maintained by the cerebral sensory input.

the selective-attention effects in the ERPs are due to a cerebral matching process which is sensitive to the similarity between the sensory input to be attended and the “attentional representation’ of this input.

PN reflects the operation of a stimulus-selection mechanism which is not only sensitive to physical stimulus parameters but is also capable to select a target stimulus in an environment of similar nontarget stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to elicit a selective-attention effect even in a situation where the stimuli to be processed and ignored are physically very similar.
the selective-attention effects can be observed in ERPs even if the stimuli to be selected do not differ in physical characteristics from the other stimuli.
the processing negativity is not a selective attention phenomenon but a more general mechanism of stimulus selection.
